title: Explain the API Gateway pattern and its responsibilities.
shortTitle: The API Gateway pattern and its responsibilities

s1_definition.profdef: The API Gateway pattern is a structural microservices pattern where a dedicated service acts as the single reverse-proxy entry point between external clients and the internal services. Its responsibilities are strictly cross-cutting: request routing, protocol translation, authentication and authorization, response aggregation and composition, rate limiting and throttling, caching, request and response transformation, observability such as logging and tracing, and resilience such as circuit breaking and retries. The pattern deliberately keeps all business logic out of the gateway so it remains a thin, generic edge layer.
s1_definition.analogy: The API Gateway pattern is like having one official reception and security desk for the entire National Bank of India head office. Every visitor, whether Rajesh coming for a loan or Priya coming about her current account, enters through that one desk. The desk checks IDs, logs who came in and when, limits crowding, and sends each person to the right department. The desk never actually approves a loan or moves money, that is the department's job. It only manages access and direction.
s1_definition.oneliner: The API Gateway pattern puts one thin edge service in front of all your services to own every cross-cutting concern, and nothing that is business logic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The API Gateway pattern is a structural microservices pattern where a dedicated service acts as the single reverse-proxy entry point between external clients and the internal services. Its responsibilities are strictly cross-cutting: request routing, protocol translation, authentication and authorization, response aggregation and composition, rate limiting and throttling, caching, request and response transformation, observability such as logging and tracing, and resilience such as circuit breaking and retries. The pattern deliberately keeps all business logic out of the gateway so it remains a thin, generic edge layer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The API Gateway pattern is like having one official reception and security desk for the entire National Bank of India head office. Every visitor, whether Rajesh coming for a loan or Priya coming about her current account, enters through that one desk. The desk checks IDs, logs who came in and when, limits crowding, and sends each person to the right department. The desk never actually approves a loan or moves money, that is the department's job. It only manages access and direction.

**One line to remember:** The API Gateway pattern puts one thin edge service in front of all your services to own every cross-cutting concern, and nothing that is business logic.

sections.s2_technical:
The first responsibility is routing, also called request forwarding. The gateway inspects the incoming request, usually the path, host, or header, and forwards it to the matching service. A predicate such as path equals the accounts prefix maps to the account service. This is the foundation on which every other responsibility is layered.

The second responsibility is protocol and payload translation. External clients often speak REST over HTTP, while internal services may speak gRPC or use a different message shape. The gateway can translate an external REST call into an internal gRPC call, or reshape a response so the client gets a clean, stable contract even as internal services evolve.

The third responsibility is security, meaning authentication and authorization. The gateway verifies the caller's token once at the edge, confirms the signature and expiry, and passes a trusted identity context to the services, for example by injecting an `X-User-Id` header after decoding the JWT. Services then trust that header rather than re-validating the token.

The fourth responsibility is composition or aggregation. For a client view that needs data from several services, the gateway can call all of them and merge the results into one response, so the client makes one call instead of many. This is the Backend-for-Frontend idea when tailored per client type.

The fifth responsibility is traffic management: rate limiting, throttling, and quotas protect services from overload and enforce fair use across tenants. The sixth is caching of slowly changing responses at the edge to cut latency and backend load. The seventh is observability: the gateway is the natural place to assign a correlation ID, log every request and response, and emit metrics and traces so a request can be followed across the whole system.

The eighth responsibility is resilience: timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers so a failing downstream service fails fast with a graceful fallback instead of hanging the edge. For example, wrapping a downstream call in a circuit breaker means when the card service is down the gateway returns a cached or default response rather than blocking.

The crucial design constraint, and the most common senior interview point, is what the gateway must not do. It must not contain business logic, must not own data, and must not become a place where teams dump orchestration. If it does, it turns into a distributed monolith and a single point of failure. The pattern's value comes precisely from the gateway staying thin and generic. In large systems you often run multiple gateways, one per client type, or split the edge into an edge gateway plus internal service meshes, so no single gateway carries everything.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a clean, stable external contract for its mobile app, but internally the services change often: one is REST, one speaks a different internal shape, and new services are added regularly. If the app talks to each service directly, every internal change breaks the app. We need a layer that owns the external contract and shields clients from internal churn. That is the gateway pattern's routing and transformation responsibility.

Problem 2 — Each responsibility of the gateway should be pluggable, because the security team, the traffic team, and the observability team all want to add behavior at the edge without rewriting the core. This maps directly to the gateway's filter-chain design, where each responsibility is a filter applied in order.

The connection to the fix: we will model the gateway pattern as an ordered chain of filters, each representing one responsibility. A request passes through a tracing filter, an authentication filter, a rate-limit filter, and finally a routing filter that forwards to the backend. This makes the pattern's responsibilities concrete and shows how they compose.

What the code will do. There is a `GatewayFilter` interface with one method. There are concrete filters: `TracingFilter`, `AuthFilter`, `RateLimitFilter`, and `RoutingFilter`. There is a `FilterChain` that runs filters in order and short-circuits when one rejects the request. There is a `RequestContext` carrying the path, token, client ID, assigned correlation ID, and the final response. The demo pushes a valid request through the full chain and an invalid one that is stopped by the auth filter.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two requests: a valid account request from Rajesh with a good token, and a payment request from Priya with a bad token.

Step 1. The valid request enters the chain. The tracing filter assigns a correlation ID, logs the path, and returns true to continue. The request now carries a correlation ID that will follow it everywhere.

Step 2. The auth filter checks the token, which is valid, logs success, and returns true. Nothing about the request changes except that it is now trusted.

Step 3. The rate-limit filter increments Rajesh's count to one, which is under the max of three, so it returns true. The request continues.

Step 4. The routing filter matches the accounts prefix, selects the account service, sets a success response that includes the correlation ID, and returns true. The chain completes and the response is a 200 from the account service.

Step 5. The invalid request enters the chain. The tracing filter assigns a correlation ID and continues. The auth filter checks the token, finds it invalid, sets the response to 401, and returns false. The chain stops immediately at the auth filter, so the rate-limit and routing filters never run and the payment service is never touched. The response is 401.

```
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] === Valid request through full chain ===
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] [trace a1b2c3d4] /api/v1/accounts/SAV2001
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] Routed to account-service
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] Response: 200 OK from account-service [trace a1b2c3d4]
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] === Invalid token stopped by AuthFilter ===
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] [trace e5f6a7b8] /api/v1/payments/pay
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [WARNING] Auth failed client=priya
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [WARNING] Chain stopped at AuthFilter
2026-10-24 12:50:01 [INFO] Response: 401 Unauthorized
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The API Gateway pattern is a structural microservices pattern where one dedicated edge service becomes the single entry point between external clients and all the internal services. Its responsibilities are strictly the cross-cutting ones: routing requests to the right service, translating protocols and reshaping payloads, authenticating and authorizing callers, aggregating responses from several services, rate limiting and throttling, caching, observability like logging and tracing, and resilience like circuit breaking and retries. The defining rule of the pattern is that every one of those is a cross-cutting concern, and the gateway deliberately holds no business logic at all.

The cleanest way I think about the pattern is as an ordered chain of filters, where each responsibility is one filter. In my banking work at National Bank of India, a request flows through a tracing filter that stamps it with a correlation ID, then an authentication filter that verifies the token once at the edge, then a rate-limit filter that protects the services from overload, and finally a routing filter that forwards the request to the right service. If any filter rejects the request, the chain stops immediately, so an unauthenticated call to the payment service is turned away at the edge and the payment service never even sees it.

This design is what gives the pattern its two big benefits. First, it decouples clients from the internal layout, because the app talks to one stable address and contract while the services behind it can change, scale, or even switch protocols without the app noticing. Second, it removes duplicated edge logic, because authentication, rate limiting, and tracing live in one place instead of being copy-pasted into every service.

The point I always emphasize in interviews is the boundary of the pattern, meaning what the gateway must not do. It must not own business logic, must not own data, and must not become a dumping ground for orchestration, because the moment it does, it turns into a distributed monolith and a single point of failure, which is exactly what microservices were meant to avoid. So in a healthy system the gateway stays thin and generic, and for very different client types I run more than one gateway, following the Backend-for-Frontend idea, so each client gets a tailored edge without any single gateway carrying everything.

---

keyPoints: Single entry point for all client requests
Cross-cutting: auth, rate limiting, routing, caching
Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway
Request tracing, circuit breaking at the edge
